events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbit
events.blurb: A 58-centimeter aluminum sphere carrying four radio antennas was boosted into an elliptical low Earth orbit, becoming the first artificial satellite. Its rhythmic beeping was receivable by amateur radio operators worldwide for 21 days.

events.title: First Human in Orbit
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet Air Force pilot rode a modified intercontinental ballistic missile into a single orbit reaching 327 km altitude, completing one lap of Earth in 108 minutes before ejecting from his capsule at 7 km and parachuting separately to a field in southern Russia. The mission was fully automated; Gagarin held an emergency manual-control key sealed in an envelope in case he needed it.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1961 — Vostok 1. Gagarin was chosen partly because he was 1.57 m tall and fit the cramped capsule. He shouted "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") at liftoff — the same casual phrase Russian pilots use to start any flight. The module didn't fully separate and sent him spinning at 8 Gs before a wire bundle burned through.

events.title: First Spacewalk
events.blurb: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and spent 12 minutes and 9 seconds in open space — the first human extravehicular activity. His spacesuit then ballooned in the vacuum to the point where he could no longer fit back through the hatch, forcing him to bleed pressure from a valve before squeezing inside headfirst.
events.revealBlurb: March 18, 1965 — Voskhod 2. The suit's engineers had fitted it with a built-in suicide pill. Leonov later said sweat filled his boots to the knee from the exertion of forcing himself back in. The spacecraft also drifted into an unplanned orbit and landed 386 km off target in the Ural mountains, where the crew spent a night in wolf country.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: Grand Tour Launch
events.blurb: A Titan IIIE rocket launched a 722-kilogram probe carrying a gold-plated phonograph record with greetings in 55 languages and 116 images. Its trajectory used gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn to reach escape velocity.

events.title: Rome Founded
events.blurb: Roman tradition records that a single founder plowed a sacred furrow around the Palatine Hill, killed his twin brother for leaping over the boundary, and established a settlement on seven hills beside the Tiber. The city's Latin name derives from that founder.

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.blurb: A force of 10,000 Athenian and Plataean hoplites defeated a Persian expedition of 25,000 troops and cavalry on a coastal plain 40 kilometres northeast of Athens. The Athenian commander had tricked the Persians into overextending on the wings, then enveloped them. The Greek victory preserved Athenian independence against the greatest military empire of the age and, by extension, the classical Greek cultural project. A runner dispatched to Athens with news of the victory is said to have expired on arrival.
events.revealBlurb: c. September 12, 490 BCE. Commander: Miltiades. The runner Pheidippides is the foundation myth of the marathon road race; the distance — 42.195 km — matches the run from the battlefield to Athens only coincidentally, set for the 1908 London Olympics.

events.title: Death of Alexander the Great
events.blurb: A Macedonian king who had conquered territory from Greece to northwest India died after a two-week fever in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in Babylon, aged 32. His generals immediately divided his empire into competing successor kingdoms, triggering a half-century of wars called the Wars of the Diadochi.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Patented
events.blurb: A textile worker patented a multi-spindle spinning frame that allowed a single operator to spin eight threads simultaneously — a number later increased to 120. The machine slashed the cost of cotton yarn and displaced the hand-spinning cottage industry within a generation.

events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Completed
events.blurb: The steamship Great Eastern finished laying 4,000 kilometres of insulated copper wire across the floor of the Atlantic, connecting Valencia Island, Ireland, to Heart's Content, Newfoundland. The first commercial message crossed in minutes — a journey that had previously taken ten days by ship.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: German Surrender at Stalingrad
events.blurb: The surviving remnants of Germany's Sixth Army — 91,000 soldiers including 24 generals and a field marshal — surrendered to Soviet forces after a 163-day battle fought street by street and building by building. Total casualties on both sides exceeded 800,000, making it the deadliest single battle in human history.

events.title: D-Day Normandy Landings
events.blurb: 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five code-named beaches along an 80-kilometre stretch of Normandy coast, supported by 11,000 aircraft sorties and 7,000 naval vessels. It was the largest amphibious invasion in history, establishing a western front in German-occupied France.

events.title: Hiroshima Atomic Bombing
events.blurb: A single B-29 bomber released a uranium fission device that detonated 580 metres above a city of 350,000 people, generating a fireball briefly hotter than the sun's surface. The explosion and resulting firestorm killed between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, with radiation deaths raising the total to approximately 140,000 by year's end.

events.title: V-E Day: Germany Surrenders
events.blurb: Germany's unconditional surrender formally took effect at midnight, ending six years of armed conflict in the European theater. Spontaneous celebrations erupted across Allied cities, with crowds estimated at one million gathering in London and jubilant crowds filling the streets of every capital.

events.title: Galileo Maps the Moon
events.blurb: An Italian natural philosopher directed a 20× magnification tube skyward and produced detailed drawings of the Moon's surface, revealing mountains and craters rather than a perfect celestial sphere as ancient philosophy held. He calculated the heights of lunar mountains by measuring the lengths of the shadows they cast.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Radium Announced
events.blurb: A husband-and-wife chemistry team announced the isolation of a new radioactive element extracted from several tonnes of pitchblende ore, reporting it was approximately 900 times more radioactive than uranium. The woman researcher would go on to become the first person to win two Nobel Prizes in different scientific disciplines.

events.title: Penicillin Discovered
events.blurb: Returning from vacation, a bacteriologist noticed a petri dish of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mold that had dissolved the surrounding bacterial colonies into clear halos. He cultured the mold — Penicillium notatum — and determined it produced a substance lethal to bacteria, naming it penicillin.

events.title: DNA Double Helix Published
events.blurb: A two-page letter in the journal Nature described a double-helical structure for deoxyribonucleic acid, with two chains running in opposite directions held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. The authors noted their structure immediately suggested a mechanism by which genetic information could be copied.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1953 — Watson and Crick, aided by Rosalind Franklin's unpublished X-ray diffraction image known as "Photo 51". Their famous closing line: "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism" — one of science's great understatements.

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer Launched
events.blurb: A technology corporation released a personal computer based on an Intel processor running an operating system licensed from a small software company for $25,000. Its open architecture allowed third-party manufacturers to build compatible clones, spawning a global personal computer industry worth trillions within a decade.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Jesse Owens Wins First Berlin Gold
events.blurb: An American sprinter from Alabama won the first of four gold medals at the Berlin Summer Games, finishing the 100-metre dash in 10.3 seconds before 110,000 spectators. He went on to win gold in the 200 metres, long jump, and 4×100-metre relay — shattering the narrative that the host nation's athletes would dominate.

events.title: Bannister Breaks the Four-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old British medical student completed a one-mile race at Oxford's Iffley Road track in 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, becoming the first person to run the distance in under four minutes. His two pacemakers dropped off with 300 yards remaining, leaving him to finish the final stretch alone before collapsing at the tape.

events.title: Mark Spitz Wins Seventh Munich Gold
events.blurb: An American swimmer won his seventh gold medal of the Munich Games by anchoring the 4×100-metre medley relay team, setting a world record in every individual event he entered. No athlete had ever won more gold medals at a single Olympic Games, and he set or broke a world record in each of his seven finals.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes Tennis Match
events.blurb: A 29-year-old professional tennis player defeated a 55-year-old former Wimbledon champion in straight sets before a crowd of 30,000 at the Houston Astrodome and a television audience of 90 million. The retired player had publicly declared that no woman could defeat him, offering a $100,000 prize to any who tried.

events.title: Secretariat Wins the Triple Crown
events.blurb: A three-year-old chestnut colt won the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in a world-record time of 2 minutes 24 seconds, becoming the first Triple Crown winner in 25 years. His margin of victory and track record remain unmatched; television viewers watching the broadcast described the race as looking like a different event from the others.

events.title: Pac-Man Reaches North America
events.blurb: A Japanese arcade cabinet featuring a yellow circular character navigating a maze while consuming dots and evading four coloured ghosts began distribution across North American arcades. Within 18 months it had been installed in over 100,000 locations and grossed more revenue than all theatrical box office receipts in America that year combined.

events.title: MTV First Broadcast
events.blurb: A music video channel began broadcasting at 12:01 a.m., opening with a brief spoken introduction before playing a three-minute clip of a rock band performing against footage of a rocket launch. The first words spoken on air were "Ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll" — the channel ran continuously for 24 hours with no advertisements.

events.title: Thriller Album Released
events.blurb: A recording artist released a 42-minute album featuring nine tracks, seven of which became top-ten singles on the Billboard Hot 100 — a chart achievement never matched before or since. The album sold more than 66 million copies, and its 14-minute title-track music video transformed the medium from a promotional clip into an art form.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Completed
events.blurb: A German goldsmith completed printing a 1,286-page Latin Bible using a press with movable metal type, producing an estimated 180 copies at a rate no scribe could approach. Each sheet required individually set letter blocks cast in an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — making it the first book in Europe produced by mechanical movable type.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Reaches India
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Portuguese captain, after a 10-month voyage south around the southern tip of Africa and up its eastern coast, dropped anchor at a spice port on the Malabar coast of India. He had sailed further than any previous European expedition. The local ruler was unimpressed by the trinkets he offered as tribute, but the sea route to Asian spices — breaking the Venetian and Arab overland monopoly — was now open.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1498 — Vasco da Gama at Calicut (Kozhikode), India. His expedition had left Lisbon with 170 men; 54 returned alive. He would make two more voyages and die in India in 1524 as the country's viceroy.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Trinity Nuclear Test
events.blurb: A plutonium implosion device was detonated atop a 30-metre steel tower in the New Mexico desert, producing a fireball visible 160 kilometres away and an explosion equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT. Watching from a bunker 16 kilometres distant, the project's scientific director later recalled a verse from Hindu scripture about becoming death, destroyer of worlds.

events.title: NATO Founded
events.blurb: Twelve nations from both sides of the Atlantic signed a mutual defense treaty in Washington, D.C., committing that an armed attack against one would be considered an attack against all. The alliance was built around Article 5 — a collective defense clause that has been invoked exactly once in its history, after 9/11.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1949 — founding members included the US, UK, France, Canada, and eight others. Lord Ismay, its first Secretary General, quipped its purpose was "to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down."

events.title: Berlin Wall Construction Begins
events.blurb: East German soldiers and workers erected barbed-wire barricades along the full length of the border between East and West Berlin overnight, sealing the most visible escape route from the Eastern Bloc without advance public announcement. Within days, temporary barriers were replaced with concrete, dividing families who had crossed freely just the day before.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: Battle of Gettysburg Begins
events.blurb: Confederate soldiers advancing through a Pennsylvania town accidentally encountered Union cavalry, triggering three days of fighting that became the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. A total of approximately 50,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, or went missing — roughly one in three of all combatants engaged on both sides.

events.title: Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Workers from the Union Pacific (building west from Nebraska) and Central Pacific (building east from California) met at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory that spring, driving a ceremonial golden spike to mark the completion of a 1,912-mile continuous rail link across the continent. The railroad cut cross-country travel from months to about a week and accelerated the mass settlement of the West at devastating cost to Native peoples.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The golden spike was immediately removed; the real spikes were iron. Chinese laborers, who built much of the Central Pacific line through the Sierra Nevada, were not invited to the ceremony. Within 25 years, four more transcontinental lines would be completed.

events.title: Women's Suffrage Amendment Certified
events.blurb: The U.S. Secretary of State certified the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment, prohibiting any state from denying the right to vote on account of sex. The amendment's passage followed a 72-year organised campaign that had begun at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, when most of its original signatories were ridiculed for the demand.
